procedural_history.impugned_order: Final Judgment and Order dated 18.05.2016 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench, Lucknow in Special Appeal No.406 of 2014.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A Single Judge of the Allahabad High Court directed that the respondent shall be taken back in service. The judgment of the Single Judge was upheld in a Special Appeal by a Division Bench of the High Court on 18 May 2016.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed the High Court's judgment. Leave to appeal was granted on 16 September 2016, and an interim suspension of the High Court's judgment was ordered. The Supreme Court heard the appeal for final hearing with the consent of both parties.

directions: There shall be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in entertaining a challenge to an order of termination after the employee had accepted the termination and sought a fresh appointment by undertaking to waive any claims related to his past service.

facts: An employee was appointed on a temporary basis as a Livestock Development Assistant.
His services were terminated after a First Information Report (FIR) was registered against him for murder (Section 302 IPC).
The employee was later acquitted by the Sessions Court.
Following his acquittal, the employee sought a fresh appointment and provided an unequivocal undertaking that he would not make any claim related to his prior service.
He was given a fresh appointment on the specific condition that he would not be entitled to the benefit of his past service.
Years later, the employee filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the original termination order and seeking continuity of service.
The High Court's Single Judge and later the Division Bench ruled in the employee's favor, setting aside the termination order and granting him continuity of service.
law: The central legal principle applied is that an individual cannot challenge a state of affairs that they have previously accepted, especially when they have received a benefit based on that acceptance. This is related to the doctrines of waiver and estoppel.
application: The Supreme Court focused on the employee's actions after his acquittal. He had consciously chosen to seek a new appointment rather than challenge his termination.
Crucially, he provided an "unequivocal undertaking" to give up any claims related to his past service in order to secure the new job.
By accepting the termination and then securing a fresh appointment based on this waiver, the employee was no longer entitled to challenge the original termination order.
The Court reasoned that such a challenge was "not open to the respondent and could not have been entertained" once he had accepted the termination and waived his rights.

Therefore, the Supreme Court found that the High Court's Single Judge and Division Bench were in "manifest error" for allowing the writ petition and setting aside the termination order in the face of the employee's clear undertaking.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in entertaining the employee's challenge to the termination order. Because the employee had accepted his termination and secured a fresh appointment by explicitly undertaking to waive any claims from his past service, he was bound by that agreement and could not later challenge the termination. The Supreme Court, therefore, allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's judgment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in entertaining a challenge to an order of termination after the employee had accepted the termination and sought a fresh appointment by undertaking to waive any claims related to his past service.
appellant_arguments: The respondent gave an unequivocal undertaking on 7 February 1989, agreeing to forego the benefit of his past services when he sought appointment as a fresh candidate.
Having been appointed on the basis of this undertaking, it was not open for the respondent to later resile from the consequences of his request being accepted.

A challenge to the termination was not open to the respondent and should not have been entertained by the court after he had accepted the termination and sought fresh appointment by waiving claims to past service.
The High Court (both the Single Judge and the Division Bench) erred in allowing the writ petition and setting aside the termination in the face of this unequivocal undertaking.
respondent_arguments: The High Court (both the Single Judge and the Division Bench) justifiably granted the benefit of his past service.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An individual who has accepted their termination and secured a fresh appointment by giving an unequivocal undertaking to waive any claims related to their past service is precluded from subsequently challenging the original termination order.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that a challenge to a termination order was not open to an employee and should not have been entertained by the courts after he had accepted the termination and consciously sought a fresh appointment by giving an unequivocal undertaking to waive any claims related to his past service. Having been appointed on the basis of that specific condition, it was not open for the employee to later resile from the consequences of his request being accepted, and the High Court was in manifest error for allowing him to do so.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the principle that a party is bound by their own 'unequivocal undertaking.' When a person consciously makes a clear promise or waiver to gain a benefit (in this case, a fresh appointment), and that benefit is granted on the specific condition of that waiver, they cannot later go back on that promise.
why_appellant_lost: Such a challenge was not open to the respondent and could not have been entertained once he had accepted his tennination and sought fresh appointment on 7 February 1989 by undertaking to give up any claim in connection with his past service.
After his acquittal on 11 October 1985, the respondent consciously sought appointment as a fresh candidate and stated that he would not make any claim in connection with his prior service.

It was on that basis that by a communication dated 17 April 1989, he was appointed as a Livestock Extension Inspector subject to the specific condition that he would not be entitled to the benefit of past service.
why_respondent_won: In the face of the unequivocal undertaking of the respondent, the learned Single Judge erred in allowing the writ petition and in setting aside the order of tennination.
The Division Bench, in the special appeal,was in error in affirming the order of the Single Judge.
The learned Single Judge was manifestly in error in entertaining a challenge to the order of termination dated 9 April 1984.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning upholds the principle that a party cannot resile from an unequivocal undertaking after having received the benefit sought through that undertaking, ensuring the integrity and finality of such agreements.
